title: When more children share one roti, what happens to each share?
description: A photo of a home kitchen opens the video, then one roti is drawn and shared first between two children and then among more. The video stops on the question of how big one share is, with no answer shown.
teaching_notes: One idea: when the same whole is shared equally, the share depends on how many share it. Ask each child to guess which share is bigger and why, and do not confirm any guess, because the next topic settles it. Watch for students who think more sharers means a bigger share.

video_script.why: Before any word of fractions, the child meets the real question: how big is one share when one whole is shared equally, and does it change when more people share it.
video_script.substitution: Picture one roti cut into equal pieces, one piece for each child.
video_script.anchor: One roti shared equally between two children, and then among more children: how big is each share?

names.Jia: talks about sharing rotis in the opening of the chapter
names.Leeza: talks about sharing rotis with the first child in the opening

never_show: a tick or cross on either share
maths_rules: One roti is the whole; every cut makes equal pieces.
First it is shared between two children, then among more children; the pieces are drawn without numbers or labels.
The open question: how big is one share when more children share the same roti. It is never answered or hinted.
video_script.design: One idea: an equal share depends on how many share the whole. Assumes nothing. Wrong idea: none is broken. The photo sits as a dimmed backdrop in the first beat and fades before the drawn roti arrives; the roti stays to the end.
